title: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring (1.4)
hook: before anything else exists, the self says its first words, then feels its first fear, then its first loneliness
tomorrow: the self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gods auditioned every sense to sing, and only the plain breath couldn't be pierced. Your line was breath is untouched by evil. Did one breath stop one sentence? Day three hundred sixty-three.

A knock on a door. Someone inside calls: who is it? And the answer often comes before any name: it's me. A small habit, easy to miss. The Brihadaranyaka stops to explain it, in the middle of telling how the world began. That habit, it says, goes all the way back to the first moment there was anyone at all. Today, the first words ever spoken, and the two feelings that came right after them.
screen: `WHO IS IT?` → `IT'S ME.` → `THE FIRST WORDS EVER SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Chapter one, section four. In the beginning, the text says, there was only the self, in the shape of a person. It looked around and saw nothing but itself. And the first thing it said was aham asmi. I am. So it came to be called I. That's why, the text adds, when anyone is called even now, they first say it's me, and then say whatever other name they have. Then something happened. The self was afraid. That's why, the text says, a person alone is afraid. And then it thought: there's nothing here but me. What am I afraid of? And the fear left. Because, the text says, fear only comes from a second. Then the self had no joy. That's why a person alone has no joy. And it wanted a second. Three moods in a few lines: I am, then fear, then longing. Notice which one thinking can cure. Fear goes the moment the self sees there's nothing else to fear. Loneliness doesn't go that way. It turns into wanting, and the wanting, tomorrow, becomes a whole world. Later Hindu philosophy uses this same little word, aham, in two very different ways. Ahamkara, the I-maker, is the ego that says me, mine, my name. And in Advaita Vedanta, the phrase aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from a few lines later in this same chapter, points at an I with no name tacked on after it. The first words in this story come before either reading: just I am, before any other name arrives.
screen: `AHAM ASMI: I AM.` · `FEAR COMES FROM A SECOND.` · `ALONE, IT HAD NO JOY.` · `TWO KINDS OF I.` · then, large: `I AM, BEFORE ANY NAME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes before the name. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice the plain sense that you're here. Not your name, not your job, not whose child or parent you are. Just: I am. If a worry comes, do what the self did in the story. Ask it gently: what, in this room, right now, is there to be afraid of? See whether the fear has anywhere to stand. Then come back to I am. The bell holds the time.
Aham asmi. I am. In the Brihadaranyaka, the first words the self ever spoke, before there was anything else to speak to.
Your line: aham asmi. Today, the next time you say it's me, at a door or on the phone, hear the two words before your name. Day three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Students of the Upanishads read this passage as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account; in Vedanta teaching it is often paired with aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from the same chapter (1.4.10), one of the great sayings.

match.prompt: the self's first moments — tap the pairs.
pairs: why we say it before our name

myth: the self's very first words in this story are "I am"
aham asmi. so, the text says, it came to be called I.
the self's fear goes away when a second being appears
it goes when the self sees there's nothing but itself: fear comes from a second.
the text explains why people say "it's me" before their name
it traces the habit back to the self's first words.

fork.setup: you are the self at the very beginning. you look around and there is nothing but you, and you're afraid. what do you do?
options: make something else to keep you company.
ask: there's nothing here but me, so what am I afraid of?
fork.reveal: the self reasons it through, and the fear leaves: fear only comes from a second. the loneliness, though, stays, and that's what makes it want a second.

original.note: Sanskrit: aham, I + asmi, am. the same aham is inside ahamkara, the I-maker, the ego.

trapdoor: what you thought: "I am" is just a grammar lesson.
what it means: in the Brihadaranyaka, the first words the self speaks, followed at once by fear, which reasoning cures, and loneliness, which it doesn't.
what a scholar hears: aham asmi (1.4.1) and, a few lines on, aham brahma asmi (1.4.10), which Advaita counts among the great sayings.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.2–3 (fear comes from a second; no joy alone)

notes: 1.4.1 in Sanskrit reads 'so 'ham asmi ity agre vyāharat'; the script gives the core words aham asmi. Confirm.
'When anyone is called, they first say it's me and then the other name': paraphrase of the end of 1.4.1. Confirm wording.
'Fear comes from a second' (dvitīyād vai bhayaṃ bhavati, 1.4.2) paraphrased.
Ahamkara described as the I-maker, the ego (as in Samkhya and the Gita); aham brahma asmi located at 1.4.10. Confirm.
